GC.35.stem: The legal process by which a foreign-born person becomes a U.S. citizen is called:

choices.text: naturalization
apportionment
ratification
cloture

GC.35.reteach: Reteach the naturalization steps (residency, application, interview, test, oath); define the term with a Frayer model.

distractor_tags.label: B
distractor_tags.rationale: Prior-knowledge error — apportionment is dividing House seats, not gaining citizenship.

distractor_tags.label: C
distractor_tags.rationale: Prior-knowledge error — ratification is approving a law or amendment.

distractor_tags.label: D
distractor_tags.rationale: Prior-knowledge error — cloture ends a Senate filibuster.

GC.35.key_rationale: Naturalization is the legal process by which a foreign-born person becomes a citizen.
GC.35.dok_rationale: Recall of a single vocabulary term.
GC.35.blooms_rationale: Student retrieves the definition of naturalization.

GC.10.stem: What change did the 17th Amendment (1913) make to how U.S. senators reach office?

choices.text: It shortened Senate terms from six years to two
It increased each state's senators from two to three
It shifted the election of senators from state legislatures to the voters
It removed the Senate's power to confirm appointments

GC.10.reteach: Reread Amendment XVII; contrast pre-1913 (legislatures chose senators) with the direct popular vote today.

distractor_tags.label: A
distractor_tags.rationale: Nearby error — term length was unchanged at six years.

distractor_tags.label: B
distractor_tags.rationale: Misconception about the number of senators per state.

distractor_tags.label: D
distractor_tags.rationale: Prior-knowledge error — confirmation power was not affected.

GC.10.key_rationale: The 17th Amendment moved the choice of senators from state legislatures to a direct vote of the people.
GC.10.dok_rationale: Requires explaining the substance of a constitutional change, not naming it.
GC.10.blooms_rationale: Student explains what the 17th Amendment changed.

GC.11.stem: Why is the Supreme Court's decision in Baker v. Carr (1962) considered a turning point for representation?

choices.text: It abolished the decennial census
It made all gerrymandering a federal crime
It ended six-year terms in the U.S. Senate
It let federal courts hear redistricting cases, opening the way to 'one person, one vote'

GC.11.reteach: Reread the Baker v. Carr holding; connect the 14th Amendment to the 'one person, one vote' standard using the TN example.

distractor_tags.label: A
distractor_tags.rationale: Prior-knowledge error — the census was untouched by the ruling.

distractor_tags.label: B
distractor_tags.rationale: Misconception — the Court made districting justiciable, not gerrymandering a crime.

distractor_tags.label: C
distractor_tags.rationale: Prior-knowledge error — Senate terms were not at issue.

GC.11.key_rationale: Baker v. Carr held that unequal districts could be challenged in federal court under the 14th Amendment, opening the way to 'one person, one vote.'
GC.11.dok_rationale: Requires analyzing the significance of a ruling for representation.
GC.11.blooms_rationale: Student analyzes why the decision reshaped representation.

GC.12.stem: Which leadership position is named in the Constitution and chosen by the majority party to lead the House of Representatives?

choices.text: The President pro tempore
The Speaker of the House
The Senate Majority Leader
The Vice President

GC.12.reteach: Build a chart of House vs. Senate leadership; note which posts the Constitution names and how each is chosen.

distractor_tags.label: A
distractor_tags.rationale: Prior-knowledge error — the President pro tempore presides in the Senate.

distractor_tags.label: C
distractor_tags.rationale: Prior-knowledge error — the Majority Leader is a Senate post, not the House's presiding officer.

distractor_tags.label: D
distractor_tags.rationale: Prior-knowledge error — the Vice President presides over the Senate.

GC.12.key_rationale: The Constitution names the Speaker of the House, who is chosen by the majority party to lead the chamber.
GC.12.dok_rationale: Requires identifying the correct post and its chamber, not simple term recall.
GC.12.blooms_rationale: Student explains which post leads the House and how it is chosen.

GC.13.stem: A Senate vote (usually 60 senators) used to end a filibuster and force a final vote is called:

choices.text: a quorum
a veto
cloture
apportionment

GC.13.reteach: Reteach the filibuster/cloture pair; map where each occurs on a 'how a bill becomes a law' flow chart.

distractor_tags.label: A
distractor_tags.rationale: Prior-knowledge error — a quorum is the minimum members needed to do business.

distractor_tags.label: B
distractor_tags.rationale: Prior-knowledge error — a veto is a presidential rejection of a bill.

distractor_tags.label: D
distractor_tags.rationale: Prior-knowledge error — apportionment divides House seats among states.

GC.13.key_rationale: Cloture is the Senate vote, usually 60 senators, that ends a filibuster.
GC.13.dok_rationale: Recall of a single procedural term.
GC.13.blooms_rationale: Student retrieves the definition of cloture.

GC.14.stem: How many U.S. Senators does Tennessee send to Congress, and why that number?

choices.text: Two, because every state gets two senators
Nine, one for each House district
A number based on its population
One, picked by the legislature

GC.14.reteach: Reteach equal Senate representation vs. population-based House seats; locate the student's own district.

distractor_tags.label: B
distractor_tags.rationale: Misconception applying House-district logic to the Senate.

distractor_tags.label: C
distractor_tags.rationale: Misconception applying population-based apportionment to the Senate.

distractor_tags.label: D
distractor_tags.rationale: Anachronism — legislative selection ended with the 17th Amendment.

GC.14.key_rationale: Every state, including Tennessee, elects exactly two U.S. Senators regardless of population.
GC.14.dok_rationale: Requires explaining the constitutional reason for the number, not only stating it.
GC.14.blooms_rationale: Student explains equal state representation in the Senate.

GC.15.stem: In McCulloch v. Maryland (1819), how did Chief Justice Marshall interpret the Necessary and Proper Clause?

choices.text: He struck it down as unconstitutional
He read it broadly, upholding Congress's implied powers
He limited Congress to only its listed powers
He gave states the power to tax the federal government

GC.15.reteach: Reread Marshall's opinion; connect the Necessary and Proper Clause to implied powers and national supremacy.

distractor_tags.label: A
distractor_tags.rationale: Misconception — the clause was upheld, not struck down.

distractor_tags.label: C
distractor_tags.rationale: Misconception — Marshall rejected the strict-construction reading.

distractor_tags.label: D
distractor_tags.rationale: Causal attribution error — the Court denied states the power to tax the national bank.

GC.15.key_rationale: Marshall read the Necessary and Proper Clause broadly, affirming Congress's implied powers.
GC.15.dok_rationale: Requires analyzing how a ruling interpreted a clause and expanded power.
GC.15.blooms_rationale: Student analyzes Marshall's interpretation of the clause.

formA.stem: Which power over citizenship does Article I give to Congress?

choices.text: The power to grant citizenship to individual applicants personally
The power to establish a uniform rule of naturalization
The power to deny citizenship to persons born in the U.S.
The power to require every citizen to pass a civics test

formA.reteach: Reread Article I, Section 8; stress 'uniform' — one national rule set by Congress.

distractor_tags.label: A
distractor_tags.rationale: Misconception — Congress sets the rule; it does not naturalize individuals one by one.

distractor_tags.label: C
distractor_tags.rationale: Misconception conflicting with 14th Amendment birthright citizenship.

distractor_tags.label: D
distractor_tags.rationale: Overgeneralization — the civics test applies to applicants, not all citizens.

formA.key_rationale: Article I gives Congress the power to establish a uniform rule of naturalization.
formA.dok_rationale: Requires identifying the specific power the clause grants, not recalling a term.
formA.blooms_rationale: Student explains the naturalization power of Congress.

formA.stem: How do the House and Senate differ in term length and size?

choices.text: House: two-year terms, larger chamber; Senate: six-year terms, smaller chamber
House: six-year terms; Senate: two-year terms
Both chambers: four-year terms, equal in size
House: life terms; Senate: two-year terms

formA.reteach: Build a House-vs-Senate comparison chart covering term length, size, and qualifications.

distractor_tags.label: B
distractor_tags.rationale: Nearby error — term lengths are reversed.

distractor_tags.label: C
distractor_tags.rationale: Misconception — the chambers differ in both term length and size.

distractor_tags.label: D
distractor_tags.rationale: Misconception — members do not serve life terms.

formA.key_rationale: The House has two-year terms and is the larger chamber; the Senate has six-year terms and is smaller.
formA.dok_rationale: Requires comparing two chambers on multiple features.
formA.blooms_rationale: Student contrasts the two chambers' terms and size.

formA.stem: For decades Tennessee did not redraw its legislative districts even as people moved to cities. What effect did this have before Baker v. Carr?

choices.text: It gave every voter exactly equal influence
It increased Tennessee's number of U.S. House seats
It ended the state's participation in the census
It made a rural vote worth far more than an urban vote

formA.reteach: Use the TN map: unchanged 1901 districts + urban growth = malapportionment; connect to Baker v. Carr.

distractor_tags.label: A
distractor_tags.rationale: Misconception — outdated districts produced unequal, not equal, influence.

distractor_tags.label: B
distractor_tags.rationale: Causal attribution error — refusing to redistrict does not add House seats.

distractor_tags.label: C
distractor_tags.rationale: Prior-knowledge error — the census continued regardless.

formA.key_rationale: Refusing to redraw districts as cities grew made rural votes count far more than urban votes.
formA.dok_rationale: Requires reasoning from a cause (frozen districts) to its effect on vote weight.
formA.blooms_rationale: Student analyzes the effect of malapportionment.

formA.stem: The Vice President presides over the Senate but may cast a vote only when:

choices.text: the Speaker of the House is absent
a bill has already been vetoed
the senators are equally divided
two-thirds of senators request it

formA.reteach: Reread Article I, Section 3; note the VP votes only to break a tie.

distractor_tags.label: A
distractor_tags.rationale: Prior-knowledge error linking the VP's role to the House.

distractor_tags.label: B
distractor_tags.rationale: Causal attribution error — a veto is unrelated to the VP's tie-breaking vote.

distractor_tags.label: D
distractor_tags.rationale: Nearby error — two-thirds is the override/expulsion threshold, not the tie rule.

formA.key_rationale: The Vice President votes in the Senate only to break a tie when senators are equally divided.
formA.dok_rationale: Requires explaining the condition for the VP's vote, not recalling the office.
formA.blooms_rationale: Student explains when the VP may vote.

formA.stem: Why does a bill face a harder path in the Senate than in the House once it reaches the floor?

choices.text: It allows extended debate, so a filibuster can stall a bill unless 60 vote for cloture
It must get the Supreme Court's approval before voting
It must pass every bill by a unanimous vote
It is not allowed to amend a bill on the floor

formA.reteach: Compare House Rules Committee limits with Senate unlimited debate; map the filibuster and cloture.

distractor_tags.label: B
distractor_tags.rationale: Misconception — courts do not pre-approve legislation.

distractor_tags.label: C
distractor_tags.rationale: Overgeneralization — the Senate does not require unanimity to pass bills.

distractor_tags.label: D
distractor_tags.rationale: Misconception — the Senate can and does amend bills.

formA.key_rationale: The Senate allows extended debate, so a filibuster can block a bill unless 60 senators invoke cloture.
formA.dok_rationale: Requires analyzing why chamber rules make Senate passage harder.
formA.blooms_rationale: Student analyzes the procedural difference between chambers.

formA.stem: Why does a U.S. Senator from Tennessee represent more people than a single U.S. Representative from Tennessee?

choices.text: A senator serves longer, so more people come to know the senator
A senator represents the whole state, not one district
A senator is chosen by the state legislature
A senator can cast two votes on each bill

formA.reteach: Contrast a senator's statewide constituency with a representative's single district; map TN's districts.

distractor_tags.label: A
distractor_tags.rationale: Causal attribution error — term length does not determine how many constituents a member has.

distractor_tags.label: C
distractor_tags.rationale: Anachronism — direct election replaced legislative selection in 1913.

distractor_tags.label: D
distractor_tags.rationale: Misconception — each senator casts one vote.

formA.key_rationale: A senator represents an entire state, while a representative serves only one district, so the senator has more constituents.
formA.dok_rationale: Requires reasoning from constituency scope, not recalling a fact.
formA.blooms_rationale: Student explains why senators have more constituents.

formA.stem: Congress created a national bank, an air force, and the interstate highway system, none of which is named in the Constitution. What constitutional basis allows this?

choices.text: The Supremacy Clause, which overrides all state laws
The Commerce Clause alone, with no other authority
Implied powers drawn from the Necessary and Proper Clause
The 17th Amendment's direct-election provision

formA.reteach: Reteach enumerated vs. implied powers; connect the Necessary and Proper Clause to McCulloch v. Maryland.

distractor_tags.label: A
distractor_tags.rationale: Prior-knowledge error — the Supremacy Clause resolves conflicts, not the source of implied powers.

distractor_tags.label: B
distractor_tags.rationale: Partial evidence — commerce is one enumerated power, but implied powers come from the Elastic Clause.

distractor_tags.label: D
distractor_tags.rationale: Prior-knowledge error — the 17th Amendment concerns Senate elections.

formA.key_rationale: Powers not listed but needed to carry out listed ones are implied powers grounded in the Necessary and Proper Clause.
formA.dok_rationale: Requires analyzing which clause justifies unlisted congressional actions.
formA.blooms_rationale: Student analyzes the source of implied powers.

formB.stem: A requirement to serve as President of the United States is being a:

choices.text: registered member of a political party
resident of Washington, D.C.
natural-born citizen
current member of Congress

formB.reteach: Reteach natural-born vs. naturalized citizen; note the presidency is limited to natural-born citizens.

distractor_tags.label: A
distractor_tags.rationale: Misconception — party membership is not a constitutional qualification.

distractor_tags.label: B
distractor_tags.rationale: Misconception — residency in the capital is not required.

distractor_tags.label: D
distractor_tags.rationale: Misconception — prior service in Congress is not required.

formB.key_rationale: Only a natural-born citizen is eligible to serve as President.

formB.stem: Before the 17th Amendment was ratified, who chose a state's U.S. senators?

choices.text: the state legislature
the state's voters directly
the House of Representatives
the President

formB.reteach: Reread Amendment XVII; contrast the old legislative selection with today's direct vote.

distractor_tags.label: B
distractor_tags.rationale: Anachronism — direct popular election began only after 1913.

distractor_tags.label: C
distractor_tags.rationale: Prior-knowledge error — the House does not select senators.

distractor_tags.label: D
distractor_tags.rationale: Prior-knowledge error — the President does not select senators.

formB.key_rationale: Before the 17th Amendment, state legislatures chose each state's U.S. senators.
formB.dok_rationale: Requires recalling the pre-amendment arrangement and understanding the change.
formB.blooms_rationale: Student explains who chose senators before 1913.

formB.stem: The redrawing of legislative district boundaries, usually after each census, is called:

choices.text: apportionment
naturalization
cloture
redistricting

formB.reteach: Reteach the census → apportionment → redistricting sequence; play the Redistrict It! grid game.

distractor_tags.label: A
distractor_tags.rationale: Nearby error — apportionment divides seats among states; redistricting draws the lines within a state.

distractor_tags.label: B
distractor_tags.rationale: Prior-knowledge error — naturalization concerns citizenship.

distractor_tags.label: C
distractor_tags.rationale: Prior-knowledge error — cloture ends a filibuster.

formB.key_rationale: Redistricting is the redrawing of district boundaries after the census.
formB.dok_rationale: Recall of a single vocabulary term.
formB.blooms_rationale: Student retrieves the definition of redistricting.

formB.stem: Which senator traditionally presides over the Senate when the Vice President is absent?

choices.text: the Speaker of the House
the Senate Minority Leader
the newest member of the Senate
the President pro tempore

formB.reteach: Chart Senate leadership; note the President pro tempore is usually the longest-serving majority senator.

distractor_tags.label: A
distractor_tags.rationale: Prior-knowledge error — the Speaker leads the House, not the Senate.

distractor_tags.label: B
distractor_tags.rationale: Nearby error — the Minority Leader guides a party, not the chamber's presiding role.

distractor_tags.label: C
distractor_tags.rationale: Misconception — seniority favors the longest-serving, not the newest, senator.

formB.key_rationale: The President pro tempore presides over the Senate in the Vice President's absence.
formB.dok_rationale: Requires identifying the correct presiding officer and its basis.
formB.blooms_rationale: Student explains who presides when the VP is away.

formB.stem: If the President vetoes a bill, how can Congress still make it become law?

choices.text: by asking the Supreme Court to overrule the veto
by passing it again with a two-thirds vote in both houses
by getting three-fourths of the states to approve it
by a simple majority in the House alone

formB.reteach: Reread Article I, Section 7; walk through the two-thirds override in both chambers.

distractor_tags.label: A
distractor_tags.rationale: Prior-knowledge error — courts do not override vetoes.

distractor_tags.label: C
distractor_tags.rationale: Nearby error — three-fourths of states is the amendment-ratification threshold.

distractor_tags.label: D
distractor_tags.rationale: Nearby error — an override needs two-thirds of both houses, not a House majority.

formB.key_rationale: Congress can override a veto with a two-thirds vote in both the House and the Senate.
formB.dok_rationale: Requires explaining the override procedure, not naming a term.
formB.blooms_rationale: Student explains how Congress overrides a veto.

formB.stem: The full group of a state's U.S. representatives together with its two senators is called its:

choices.text: delegation
cabinet
caucus
electorate

formB.reteach: Reteach delegation, constituent, and district; identify Tennessee's own delegation.

distractor_tags.label: B
distractor_tags.rationale: Prior-knowledge error — the cabinet advises the President.

distractor_tags.label: C
distractor_tags.rationale: Prior-knowledge error — a caucus is a party meeting or grouping.

distractor_tags.label: D
distractor_tags.rationale: Nearby error — the electorate is the body of voters, not the members elected.

formB.key_rationale: A state's members of Congress together make up its delegation.
formB.dok_rationale: Recall of a single vocabulary term.
formB.blooms_rationale: Student retrieves the definition of delegation.

formB.stem: The Necessary and Proper Clause is often called the 'Elastic Clause.' Why does that nickname fit?

choices.text: It shrinks the powers of Congress over time
It applies only during declared wars
It lets Congress stretch its listed powers to meet new needs
It can be removed by a presidential veto

formB.reteach: Reteach implied powers; explain how the clause 'stretches' enumerated powers, citing McCulloch v. Maryland.

distractor_tags.label: A
distractor_tags.rationale: Misconception — the clause expands rather than shrinks power.

distractor_tags.label: B
distractor_tags.rationale: Overgeneralization — the clause is not limited to wartime.

distractor_tags.label: D
distractor_tags.rationale: Misconception — a constitutional clause is not removable by veto.

formB.key_rationale: The clause is 'elastic' because it lets Congress stretch its enumerated powers to carry them out.
formB.dok_rationale: Requires analyzing the metaphor against the clause's function.
formB.blooms_rationale: Student analyzes why the clause is called 'elastic.'

_psychometric_summary.note: IRT 3PL parameters are pre-field-test design-time estimates, to be calibrated on field-test data.
